attributes.diagnose: en lille, tykkødet, fint filtet, ± opsprækkende rørhat med okkerbrun, honninggul til brunoliven hat og stok og bleggule til okkerbrune rørmundinger. Stokken er tilspidsende og uensartet ru på overfladen. Overflader og kød uden eller kun med svage blånende reaktioner. De ± tenformede sporer måler 12-17,5 x 4-5,5 μm. Den snylter på almindelig bruskbold (Scleroderma citrinum), gerne i fugtige birkemoser, men uden at gøre synderlig skade. Den hævdes også at kunne gro på andre arter af bruskbold. Detaljerne omkring det parasitiske forhold mellem de to svampearter kendes endnu ikke. Det er imidlertid påfaldende, at den snyltende rørhat er meget stedfast: de samme mycelier af bruskbolde angribes år efter år mens de omgivende mycelier går fri. Dette kunne tyde på, at parasitismen primært foregår på mycelie-niveau.
attributes.forvekslingsmuligheder: Voksemåden med frugtlegemer direkte fra frugtlegemerne af bruskbolde er enestående. En nærtstående art, P. astraeicola, der snylter på barometerstjerne (Astraeus), er kendt fra bl.a. Japan.
attributes.oekologi: Snyltende rørhat vokser på almindelig bruskbold (Scleroderma citrinum), men kan også træffes på andre arter af brusakbold. der vokser i løv- og nåleskove, især på tørvebund. Snyltende rørhat findes hist og her i Danmark.
attributes.DK_reference: H. Knudsen i L. Hansen & H. Knudsen, Nordic Macromycetes 2: 60, 1992.

Den snylter på almindelig bruskbold (Scleroderma citrinum), gerne i fugtige birkemoser, men uden at gøre synderlig skade. Den hævdes også at kunne gro på andre arter af bruskbold. Det er imidlertid påfaldende, at den snyltende rørhat er meget stedfast: de samme mycelier af bruskbolde angribes år efter år mens de omgivende mycelier går fri. attributes.bogtekst_gyldendal_en:
Pseudoboletus parasiticus is a small, thick-fleshed, finely felty, ± cracking bolete with a cinnamon-buff, honey-yellow to brownish-olive cap and stem, and pale yellow to yellowish-brown pores. The stem ± tapers towards the base and has an unevenly roughened surface. Surfaces and flesh either do not stain blue or only stain faintly blue. The ± fusiform spores measure 12–17.5 × 4–5.5 µm. Parasitizes Scleroderma citrinum, mostly in damp Betula forests, but does not appear to cause obvious harm to the fruitbodies of the host. It has also been reported as occurring on other species of Scleroderma.
Distinctive and unlikely to be misidentified. A closely related species, P. astraeicola, parasitizes species of Astraeus and is known from, e.g., Japan.
Widespread, occasional to rather rare and virtually absent from the hemiboreal–boreal zones; July–November.
The details concerning this species’ parasitism are not well understood. It is striking how site-faithful it is, and frutibodies will appear from the same Scleroderma mycelium year after year, while neighbouring mycelia are free of frutibodies. This would indicate that the parasitism is carried out at the level of the mycelium, possibly involving the mycorrhizae of the Betula/Scleroderma association.

Imleria badia is a medium-sized bolete with an at first finely felty, but later greasy-slimy, greyish-brown to orange-brown cap. The stem is fibrillose-marbled and pale orange-brown. The fine, pale yellow pores stain blue after bruising, whereas the flesh hardly stains. The ± fusiform spores measure 12–15 × 4–5 µm. Occurs predominantly with conifers on poor soils, but also with Fagus on mor soils.
The most similar species is Lanmaoa fragrans, which is somewhat more robust, mostly clustered and has tapering stems; it occurs with deciduous trees in more southern parts of Europe. Xerocomus, Xerocomellus and Hortiboletus generally have thinner stems, larger pores and do not have caps that become sticky with age and in wet weather. Although Suillus species are mainly sticky-slimy, the slime layer also runs down the stem and many species have a slimy ring. Due to the absence of red colours, Imleria badia may recall a species of Boletus but these have reticulate stems and the pores never stain blue.
Widespread and common; June–December.
